notes: Bench frame times for the two headless scenes are reported, not asserted: they are one machine's ops/sec and exist so a human can see whether a change moved the curve. Heap, bundle and per-template frame-time numbers ARE asserted, by alloc.test.ts, bundle-size.test.ts, template-frame-time.test.ts and tests/visual/tests/frame-time.spec.ts.

frameTime.note: `hello-cube` and `thousand-entities` are the headless `vitest bench` scenes: ops/sec on one machine, reported and not asserted. `templates` is the Phase 12 gate and IS asserted, in two places: `tests/visual/tests/frame-time.spec.ts` measures each template in Chromium on SwiftShader at 1280x720 and compares the median against `budgetMs`, and `benchmarks/template-frame-time.test.ts` asserts every recorded row against the coding-standards §7 budget. The live half is the Playwright `frame-budget` project (`pnpm test:frame-budget`), and CI runs it on `macos-latest`: these ceilings were recorded on that machine class, and GitHub's `ubuntu-latest` measures the runner rather than the engine -- 2.0 ms against a 1.0 ms ceiling for 2d-topdown, and neither 3D template able to finish 420 frames inside the 240 s per-test timeout (ADR-0009, 2026-09-07). The data half runs on every runner. First measured on `macos-latest` 2026-09-07: medians of 0.4, 0.4, 1.2 and 0.9 ms against ceilings of 1.0, 1.0, 2.0 and 2.0 -- the runner is 1.3x to 1.7x slower than the recording machine, and 3d-third-person has the least headroom at 1.7x, so it is the row to re-measure rather than relax if that job goes red with no engine change behind it.

2d-topdown.note: Five runs on 2026-09-06/07 measured medians of 0.3, 0.2, 0.3, 0.3 and 0.3 ms and worst frames between 0.9 and 1.3 ms; the row records the highest of each. The ceiling is 1.0 ms — about 3x the median, and half the 2 ms budget the standards give a 2D game. Chromium quantises performance.now() to 0.1 ms, which is a third of this median, so the spread above is mostly the clock.

2d-sidescroller.note: Five runs measured a median of 0.3 ms every time, with worst frames between 0.8 and 1.0 ms. Same ceiling and same reasoning as the top-down template; the two carry the same engine and differ only in their own gameplay code.

3d-third-person.note: Five runs measured medians of 0.7, 0.8, 0.7, 0.7 and 0.7 ms; the row records the highest. Worst frames ranged from 1.3 to 4.2 ms — the 4.2 ms outlier is a navmesh crowd update landing in the same frame as a shadow-map rebuild. The ceiling is 2.0 ms, half the 4 ms the standards give a 3D game; the worst frame is reported and not asserted, because a budget is not about a single frame.

3d-first-person.note: Five runs measured medians of 0.7, 0.9, 0.7, 0.7 and 0.7 ms; the row records the highest. Worst frames ranged from 1.3 to 1.9 ms. Same ceiling and same reasoning as the third-person template; it carries no navmesh, and its worst frame is correspondingly calmer.

hello-cube.note: The website example at website/examples/hello-cube/, not the headless `frameTime.hello-cube` bench scene above -- the two share a name and measure different things. Four runs on 2026-09-07 measured a median of 0.1 ms every time, with worst frames of 0.3, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.4 ms. 0.1 ms IS Chromium's performance.now() quantum, so the median is one clock tick and the true cost is somewhere under it: the scene is five draw calls, one shadow-casting light and one nine-line script. The ceiling is therefore 0.5 ms -- five ticks, not 2.5x a real number -- because a ceiling one tick above a one-tick median would measure the clock. It is 8x inside the 4 ms coding-standards §7 budget for a 3D scene, and a real regression here would be a factor of five. The fourth run is the one `pnpm test:frame-budget` printed on 2026-09-07 -- median 0.1 ms, worst 0.4 ms, ceiling 0.5 ms. Re-run on 2026-09-07 with the examples rebuilt for the hero rework: median 0.1 ms, worst 0.2 ms, ceiling 0.5 ms -- unchanged, as expected, since nothing in this example changed.

pbr-model.note: Re-recorded on 2026-09-07 after the hero's subject became the ignifx mascot ship (models/ignifx-ship.glb: 67,983 triangles across 12 draw calls, three 1024-pixel textures) and the composition became the key-art still in examples/pbr-model/shot.ts. The run `pnpm test:frame-budget` printed that day measured median 0.1 ms, worst 1.0 ms against the 0.5 ms ceiling -- one Chromium clock quantum, and *lower* than the 0.2 ms / 1.3 ms the corset composition it replaced recorded, which is the point worth writing down: a 68,000-triangle draw with image-based lighting, a shadow map, a bloom and an SMAA pass is GPU work, and the engine's own per-frame CPU is the same handful of components either way. Earlier runs of that composition measured medians of 0.1, 0.1, 0.1 and 0.2 ms with worst frames of 1.2, 0.5, 1.3 and 1.3 ms, so the worst frame moves around by a millisecond between runs: an image-processing recompile or a post-process pipeline creation can land inside one frame. The 0.5 ms ceiling is unchanged -- five clock ticks rather than a multiple of a one-tick median -- and it is 8x inside the 4 ms coding-standards §7 budget for a 3D scene. The worst frame is reported and not asserted: a budget is not about a single frame.

frameTime.machine: macOS 25.5 arm64 (Apple Silicon), Chromium (Playwright 1.63) + SwiftShader, 1280x720, 300 frames after a 120-frame warm-up, @babylonjs/lite 1.27.0
frameTime.swiftShaderFactorNote: Measured, and the measurement says there is no factor worth applying. Each template was run twice on 2026-09-06, once with --use-webgpu-adapter=swiftshader and once on the host GPU, and the ratio of the two mean engine-CPU figures came out 0.588, 0.429, 0.941 and 2.107 for 2d-topdown, 2d-sidescroller, 3d-third-person and 3d-first-person respectively -- i.e. SwiftShader is *cheaper* in engine CPU as often as it is dearer, because what it slows down is the rasteriser and what is being measured is the CPU side of the frame. Chromium also quantises performance.now() to 0.1 ms, which is a third of a 2D template's whole median, so the spread is mostly the clock. The ceilings below are therefore set from the SwiftShader measurement itself with about 2.5x of headroom, and every one of them is well inside the coding-standards §7 budget with no multiplier at all.

hello-cube.note: Four runs measured -186960, 60688, 60744 and 104088 bytes after a 600-step warm-up. The ceiling is 2.5x the largest.

thousand-entities.note: Three runs measured exactly 9072 bytes. 2x headroom would be 18144; the ceiling is 64 KiB because heapUsed is a whole-process number that a different V8 build can shift, and 64 KiB is still 16x under the 1 MB the standards imply and three orders of magnitude under one small object per entity per frame.

examples/hello-cube.note: gzipBytes is the entry chunk, which is what a first load actually fetches; totalGzipBytes sums all 294 emitted chunks, almost all of them dynamically imported Lite features this scene never reaches. The ceiling is the measurement x 1.1. Re-measured 2026-09-06 alongside the Phase 12 template re-record: the entry chunk moved from 270551 to 284142 bytes, +13600, from engine work in Phases 10 and 11 rather than from anything in this example -- its source did not change. The plan's Phase 2 target of 250 KB gzipped is still NOT met: the entry chunk is 284142 bytes, 34142 over. Phase 12 did not chase it; that is a packages/** job. Re-measured 2026-09-07: 284142 -> 268634 bytes; Lite's error-message table and glTF parser now load through dynamic imports (hardening, 2026-09-07); the Phase 2 target of 250000 bytes is still missed by 18634 bytes.

templates/2d-topdown.note: Re-measured 2026-09-06 after Phase 12's polish. The entry chunk grew from 1177376 to 1194522 bytes, +17154: a title screen, a pause menu, a settings screen with sliders, an interactive rebinding page, a save file and a localisation document, minus the Dialog-based pause menu they replaced. The ceiling is the new measurement x 1.1. 797097 of those bytes are still @dimforge/rapier2d-compat's dist/rapier.mjs, which inlines its WebAssembly as base64 and is statically imported by @ignifx/physics-2d; the non-Rapier remainder is about 397 KB. The Phase 2 target of 250 KB gzipped does not apply to a template that ships a physics engine. Re-measured 2026-09-07: 1194522 -> 1181179 bytes; the templates' menu front end moved into @ignifx/ui's Menu/MenuStack and core lazy-loads Lite's error table and glTF parser (hardening, 2026-09-07).

templates/2d-sidescroller.note: Re-measured the same way, on the same machine, on 2026-09-06. Within 677 bytes of the top-down template: the two carry the same packages and the same front end, and differ only in their own gameplay source. Re-measured 2026-09-07: 1195224 -> 1181820 bytes; the templates' menu front end moved into @ignifx/ui's Menu/MenuStack and core lazy-loads Lite's error table and glTF parser (hardening, 2026-09-07).

templates/3d-third-person.note: Re-measured 2026-09-06 after Phase 12's polish: 406181 -> 423698 bytes, +17451, which is the front end (title, pause, settings, rebinding, save) plus the PostProcessStack the graphics section switches. The ceiling is the new measurement x 1.1. The entry chunk is a third of a 2D template's because Havok's WebAssembly is NOT inlined: @ignifx/physics declares HavokPhysics.wasm in ignifx.assets.public and @ignifx/vite-plugin copies it into dist/assets/ unhashed (1.4 MB raw, not JavaScript, so it is in neither number here), where Rapier's rapier2d-compat inlines 797 KB of base64 straight into the 2D templates' entry. The second cost of a 3D template is Recast: recast-navigation-*.js gzips to about 453 KB and inlines its own wasm as a data: URL, but it is a separate chunk that Babylon Lite import()s only when a NavMeshSurface bakes, so it is in totalGzipBytes and not in the first-load entry. Re-measured 2026-09-07: 423698 -> 410195 bytes; the templates' menu front end moved into @ignifx/ui's Menu/MenuStack and core lazy-loads Lite's error table and glTF parser (hardening, 2026-09-07).

templates/3d-first-person.note: Re-measured the same way, on the same machine, on 2026-09-06: 405904 -> 422640 bytes. Within 1007 bytes of the third-person template. It carries the Recast chunk too even though it never bakes a navmesh: @ignifx/3d registers its NavigationService unconditionally, so Lite's navigation module is reachable and the chunk is emitted -- it is simply never fetched at runtime, which is what keeps it out of the entry number. Re-measured 2026-09-07: 422640 -> 409182 bytes; the templates' menu front end moved into @ignifx/ui's Menu/MenuStack and core lazy-loads Lite's error table and glTF parser (hardening, 2026-09-07).

twoD.machine: macOS 25.5 arm64 (Apple Silicon), Node 24.20.0, Vitest 5.0.0, @babylonjs/lite 1.27.0, Chromium (Playwright) + SwiftShader
twoD.note: S6.1. CPU milliseconds per frame with the render loop stopped (app.step), so no presented frame and no SwiftShader rasterisation is in the sample. `loaded` dirties all 1000 movers each frame; `idle` moves nothing. Reported, not asserted, except that `loadedMedianMs` must stay under the 2 ms coding-standards §7 budget and `syncedWhileIdle` must be 0. Chromium quantises performance.now() to 0.1 ms, so the browser medians are coarse.

browser.note: The camera sees 1024 of the 10000 tiles, so chunk culling is exercised.

node.note: A headless app has no surface, so there is no visible rectangle to cull against and every tile is a live sprite. This is the harder of the two measurements.

pixelPerfect.note: S6.3. Blended pixels in a full-canvas readback of a 16x16 one-pixel checkerboard: 0 means every pixel is pure magenta or pure black.
pixelPerfect.counterExampleNote: Linear-sampled atlas at zoom 6.0377 with pixelPerfect off: the whole 64x64 canvas blends.

devtools.note: Phase 10's zero-cost-when-closed exit criterion. The 1,002-entity headless scene is built four times -- plain, devtools, devtools, plain, one app alive at a time -- warmed for 120 frames and then stepped 600 times per block, and each variant's median is taken over its 1,200 samples. Five consecutive runs on 2026-09-06 measured differences of 0.0000, 0.0006, -0.0001, 0.0005 and 0.0036 ms; the row below is the fourth. An earlier two-app design is recorded in the test's header for the record: it read +0.007/+0.000/+0.016 ms with the plain app built first and -0.007/-0.004/-0.008 ms with the devtools app built first, which is construction order rather than devtools, and is why the measurement runs one app at a time.
